client_context: A 50-year-old who was sober for 3 years but relapsed after a sudden job loss. Feels deep shame and hopelessness. Has been to AA before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Dave. You can grab that chair or the couch — fair warning, the couch has a spring that's seen better days, so... chair's probably your friend. Walk-in today, yeah? No pressure, no agenda. Just — what's going on?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, uh... walk-in. My wife basically told me I had to come somewhere or she was done. So. Here I am. I don't really know what I'm supposed to say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay, so she drew a line. That's... a lot of pressure to walk in with. Before we get into anything heavy — what's your sense of it? Like, setting aside what she wants for a second, what made you actually walk through that door today instead of just sitting in your car for an hour and driving home?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't know. Maybe both. I did sit in the parking lot for like fifteen minutes, I'll be honest. But I — look, I know things are bad. I'm not gonna pretend they're not. I just... I had three years. Three years sober, went to AA, did the whole thing. And then I lost my job in November and I just... fell apart. I'm fifty years old and I fell apart like some kind of — I don't know. It's embarrassing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three years is not nothing. That's — I want to make sure that doesn't get lost in this conversation. Three years of doing something really hard. And then something massive happened, and you're sitting here calling yourself embarrassing for being human about it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I don't know. It doesn't feel like three years matters much right now. It's like... what was the point, you know? I'm right back where I started. Maybe worse, because at least before I didn't have three years to lose.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a heavy thing to carry — the feeling that it was all erased. Can I ask, what was going on inside when the job ended? Like, what happened in those first few weeks?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was a layoff. Whole department got cut. Twenty-two years at that company. Twenty-two years. And they send you an email — an email — at 7 in the morning and by noon your badge doesn't work. I just... I came home and my wife was at work and the house was quiet and I just — I don't know. I found a bottle. I'm not even sure when I decided. I just... did it. And then that was it. Five months ago. I've been drinking every day since.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty-two years, and an email. God. That's a gutpunch. You know, I'm struck by something — you said you 'found' a bottle. Like part of you was almost... watching it happen. That's not the same as choosing it, not really. That sounds like a guy who got hit by something enormous and reached for the only thing that ever made the noise stop.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's actually pretty close to what it felt like. I wasn't even — I wasn't thinking about the three years. I wasn't thinking about anything. I just... the quiet in that house was unbearable. And then it wasn't. And then I hated myself for it. But by then it was already... you know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were sober for three years — what was that like? Not in a 'you should get back to it' way, I'm just curious. What did those years give you that you remember?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I was... present. That's the word. I was at my daughter's graduation. I actually remember it — like, I was there. I was coaching her soccer team when she was little and I'd show up half in the bag, and I swore I'd never be that guy again. And for three years I wasn't. I was somebody she could — she'd call me, just to talk. She doesn't call anymore. Not since I... since this started again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me try to hold all of this together for a second. You lost a job that was a huge part of your identity — twenty-two years, gone overnight, no warning. That knocked you completely sideways, and drinking was the first thing your brain went to because it's always worked before. But at the same time, you know what you had. You know what sober felt like. Your daughter calling. Being at the graduation. Being someone you recognized. And now you're here — not just because your wife pushed you, but because some part of you remembers what you were building and isn't ready to let that go. Does that land?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... yeah. Yeah, it lands. I've been so stuck in the shame of it that I — I don't know, I forgot that I actually liked who I was. For a while there. I liked who I was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That guy hasn't gone anywhere. He got hit hard and he's been hiding, but he walked through a door today. So — no big plans, no twelve-step pep talk from me right now — what would feel like one small, true thing you could do this week? Something for him.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... I know there's a meeting Thursday nights, over on Clement Street. I used to go to that one. Saw some of the same faces every week. I could — I mean, I'd have to walk in and explain myself, which is, you know, terrifying. But I know how it works. I know those people. Maybe I go Thursday. And maybe I call my daughter. Not to explain everything, just... call her.

client_context: A 55-year-old who lost their spouse 8 months ago and has been drinking to numb the pain. Isolated from friends and family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know the drive over can feel like a lot, especially right after detox. Take whatever time you need to get comfortable.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm only here because Dr. Reyes said I had to be. I don't really... I'm not sure what I'm supposed to get out of this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're here because someone else pushed for it, not necessarily because you wanted to be. What's that like, sitting in that chair right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Annoying. I just spent two weeks in detox being told what to do, what to eat, when to sleep. And now I'm here. It's like... I'm fifty-five years old. I don't need to be managed.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You feel like your independence has been stripped away. Like everyone around you has decided they know better than you do.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. My daughter practically dragged me to detox. My son keeps calling every day like I'm some kind of... I don't know. Like I can't be trusted in my own home.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You showed up anyway. Even feeling all of that — resentment, being watched, being pushed — you're still here. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I don't know if that makes me brave or just tired of fighting everyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Maybe both. Tell me — when did you lose your husband?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Eight months ago. August. He had a heart attack. No warning, no — he was fine and then he wasn't. And everyone kept telling me, you know, 'at least it was quick, he didn't suffer.' Like that's supposed to make it better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: People said the wrong things, tried to wrap it up neatly when nothing about it was neat.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Thirty-one years. We were married thirty-one years. And now I come home to a house that's just... quiet. I started drinking to fall asleep. That's all it was at first. Just to get through the night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It started as a way to survive the nights. And somewhere along the way it became something more than that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't — look, I know it got out of hand. I'm not stupid. But it's not like I was some kind of... I was functioning. I was going to the grocery store, I was paying my bills.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You want me to know you weren't falling apart completely — that you kept things together even while you were hurting. And at the same time, you just said you know it got out of hand. Both of those things can be true.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I guess they can.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was the moment — or was there a moment — where you thought, okay, this is too much?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My granddaughter called me. She's seven. She wanted to video chat and I... I was drunk at two in the afternoon. And I almost picked up. I almost let her see me like that. I didn't, but... I almost did.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You stopped yourself. In that moment, something in you said no — not like this, not in front of her.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I put the phone down and I just sat there. And I thought, Richard would be so ashamed of me. That's — that's his name. Was. Richard.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You still carry him with you. His opinion, his values — that still matters to you deeply.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He would have — he was a good man. He would have gotten me help sooner, probably. He always knew when something was wrong with me before I did. And now he's not here to... I'm sorry. I told myself I wasn't going to cry.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Take your time. There's no wrong way to do this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm scared. That's — if I'm being honest, I'm scared that without the drinking I'm just going to have to feel all of it. All the time. And I don't know if I can do that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That fear makes complete sense. The drinking was doing a job — keeping the grief at a distance. And now you're wondering what happens when that buffer is gone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Because it's not like the grief goes away just because I stopped drinking. It's still there. It's always there. I just... I didn't want to feel it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I share something with you about that? What you're describing is something a lot of people go through after a significant loss. The grief doesn't disappear — but it does become more manageable over time when you move through it rather than around it. That's not a platitude, that's what we actually see. It's painful, but it's workable.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Workable. I haven't heard it put like that before. Everyone always says 'it gets better' and I just want to throw something at them.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would 'workable' look like for you? If you had to picture your life six months from now — not perfect, just workable — what would be different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... I'd want to call Lily back. My granddaughter. Without dreading that she'll notice something wrong with me. And maybe — I used to have a garden. I haven't touched it since August. I'd like to be someone who goes outside again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me reflect back what I'm hearing from you today. You came in feeling pushed into this, resentful, not sure it was worth your time. And somewhere in this conversation you told me about your granddaughter Lily, about Richard, about a garden you used to love. You said you're scared — but you also know what you want on the other side of that fear. That's a lot of clarity for a first session.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't expect to say all that. I came in here ready to sit with my arms crossed for an hour.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And instead you showed up. The real you — not the version that was managing everyone's worry, not the one who had everything under control. You let yourself be seen today. That took guts.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. Maybe. I think Richard would have liked you, actually. You don't talk to me like I'm broken.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not broken. You're grieving and you've been doing it alone. What would feel like a manageable first step — something small — before we meet again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe calling Lily. Or... even just going outside and looking at the garden. I don't have to do anything to it. Just look at it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Just look at it. That's enough. You're not trying to fix everything at once.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've been trying to fix everything at once for eight months. Maybe that's part of the problem. I think... I think I want to try. I don't know if I'm going to be good at this, but I want to try.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Wanting to try is the whole thing. We'll work with what's real — the grief, the fear, the garden, Lily, all of it. You don't have to have it figured out before you walk in here. Same time next week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Same time next week.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for joining me today, Gerald. I know doing this over video isn't the most natural thing, but I appreciate you showing up. Before we get into anything formal — how are you feeling right now, just in this moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh... fine, I guess. A little strange, talking to a screen. But alright. I've done stranger things.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fair enough. So you're here because of the court requirement. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But I'm genuinely curious — beyond what the judge said, what's your own sense of why you're sitting here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, I mean... the judge said I had to come. I got a DUI a couple months back. First one ever, I'll tell you that. Sixty-five years old, first run-in with the law. I wasn't even that drunk, in my mind anyway. I misjudged it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds like it caught you off guard. Not just the stop, but the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it did. I mean, I've driven after a few drinks plenty of times over the years. Nothing ever happened. I thought I knew my limits. Guess I was wrong that night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does drinking look like for you these days — like on a regular day, what does that actually look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, maybe... a few beers in the afternoon, some whiskey in the evenings. It's not like I'm falling down. I just — it passes the time. Since I retired there's a lot of time to pass.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your doctor flagged some liver concerns at your last checkup. What did you make of that when he told you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That... yeah. That scared me, I won't lie. He said my enzymes were elevated. I kind of brushed it off at the time, told him it was probably nothing. But it's been sitting in the back of my mind ever since.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What goes through your head when you let yourself think about it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm 65, I've already got the knees, the blood pressure, the whole package. And now this. I don't... I don't want to end up like my father. He drank heavy his whole life and by the end, his liver was shot. It wasn't a good way to go.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're connecting what the doctor said to what you watched happen to your father.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. He drank the same way — like it was just part of the day, nothing to think about. And I always told myself I wasn't like him. But lately... I wonder. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes real honesty to say that out loud. And I want to stay with that — you said you wonder. What does that wondering actually sound like in your head?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It sounds like... am I going down the same road? Is that what's happening here? I try not to think about it too much because it's... it's easier not to. But then another day goes by and.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me what changed when you retired. What did a regular day look like before, versus now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Before, I was up at six, at the plant by half past seven. Supervisor for 28 years. I knew what I was doing, I had people depending on me, I had a routine. My wife was still alive then too. Now I wake up and there's just... nothing scheduled. Nobody depending on me. The days are real long.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty-eight years of knowing exactly where you fit, exactly what you were for — and then retirement takes that away. And you're navigating all of it without your wife.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's about right. I thought I'd be relieved. Golf, some gardening, whatever. But it's just quiet. And the quiet, it gets to me more than I expected.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you miss most?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Feeling useful. Like what I did mattered to somebody. Even just... having somewhere to be in the morning. My wife used to say I was the kind of man who needed a job to function right. She was right about most things.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to reflect back what I'm hearing, because there's a lot here. You lost your wife, then you retired, and those two things together left a real gap — in your purpose, your identity, your daily connections. Drinking became a way to fill that gap, or at least make it quieter. And now you've got a DUI, a doctor worried about your liver, and part of you is asking whether you're heading down the same road as your father. Does that land?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... yeah. When you put it all together like that it sounds pretty bad. I knew it, I think, somewhere. I just hadn't... said it all out loud before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If things went the way you actually wanted them to — five years from now — what does that look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I haven't let myself think about that, honestly. Maybe... being around for my grandkids. I've got three of them, they're young still. I don't see them near enough. I'd like to be the kind of grandfather they actually know. Not some old man they visited a couple times before he was gone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being there for them — that matters to you in a deep way.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: More than I let on, yeah. My daughter called last month, asked how I was doing, and I said fine, everything's fine. But... I don't think she believed me. And honestly I didn't believe myself either. She knows something's wrong. She just doesn't push.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If you decided things needed to change — not just with drinking but in your life overall — what do you think would actually have to be different?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I need something to do. Something that gets me out of the house and around people. I've been thinking about volunteering at the veterans' center — I was in the Army, years ago. I looked it up once. Never called. And I think I need to stop pretending to my daughter that everything's fine. She deserves to actually know what's going on with me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're already thinking about this in a real, concrete way — not just cutting back on the drinking but actually rebuilding something. A sense of purpose, an honest relationship with your daughter. That's not nothing, Gerald.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's strange. I came in here thinking this was just a box to check for the court. I didn't expect to... I don't know. Feel like this. Like something shifted a little.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would a first step look like — something small, something you could actually do in the next week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I could call the veterans' center. I've got the number written down somewhere. I just never dialed it. And call my daughter — actually tell her what's been going on instead of giving her the everything's fine routine. Those two things.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Both of those connect to the same thing — not being alone in this anymore. That's what I'm hearing underneath it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. The drinking is the drinking. But the real problem is I've been hiding. From my family, from the world, from myself if I'm honest. And I'm tired of it. I'm tired of quiet days that feel like nothing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in today because a judge required it. But here's what I actually heard: someone who lost his wife, lost his sense of purpose, and found himself in a quieter and lonelier life than he ever planned for. Drinking became the way through the days. And now there's a doctor worried about your liver, a DUI, and a part of you that keeps wondering if you're repeating your father's story. But you also talked about your grandkids, your daughter, the veterans' center. You're not someone who wants to disappear. That's real, and that matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... I mean, that's it exactly. I just needed somebody to help me see it laid out clear like that. I knew it was there, I just kept walking past it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: As we wrap up today — what feels most alive for you right now, thinking about what comes next?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Hope, maybe. Which I haven't felt much of in a while, to tell you the truth. I think there's still time to turn this around. I'm 65, not dead. I'm not ready to give up on myself. Not yet.

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So, Marcus — can I call you Marcus? Your chart says a friend referred you in. I want to hear it from you, though — what's been going on lately?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, Dave basically dragged me here. I appreciate it, I do, but... look, I'm fine. The divorce was rough, obviously, but it's not like I've got some problem. I just — it's been a hard few months, okay? I drink a little more than usual, so what. I'm not falling apart.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A little more than usual. And Dave cared enough to pick up the phone and get you here. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Dave worries too much. We were in the Corps together — he's always been like that. [pause] Look, Carol and I were together nineteen years. Nineteen. And now I'm in a two-bedroom apartment watching SportsCenter by myself. Having a few beers to unwind at night is just... that's what guys do. That's normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Nineteen years is a long time. What do you miss most — about the life you had before all this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... hm. [long pause] My kids. Tyler's sixteen, Maya's thirteen. I used to coach Tyler's baseball. Drive Maya to her violin lessons on Saturday mornings. Now I get them every other weekend, and even that — there's so much tension with Carol that sometimes the visits just... don't happen. And I can't — I can't make that happen from the outside.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the beers at night — it sounds like it started as a way to get through the quiet. But the quiet is also where all of that lives. Missing them. The Saturday mornings.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. [exhales] Yeah, that's — I never thought about it that way. It's like the second they go home after a visit, I don't — I can't just sit there. It's too quiet. I open one beer, then another, and I'm watching ESPN at two in the morning and I don't even know how I got there. I don't even remember falling asleep.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Even with all the tension, even when the visits fall through — you keep showing up for Tyler and Maya. That matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... of course. They're my kids. [pause] Tyler asked me last month — he asked me if I was okay. He's sixteen. He shouldn't be worried about his dad. [voice tightens] That bothered me more than anything Carol's thrown at me. I keep thinking about that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was that like, hearing him ask that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Awful. Like, genuinely awful. I just kept thinking — is that what he sees? Some guy who can't hold it together? My dad wasn't around. That was the one thing I swore — I swore I would never be that guy. And I don't know... [voice quieter] I don't know how I got here. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull this together. You came in today because Dave — someone who's known you since the Corps — was worried enough to push. You've been drinking to survive some brutal nights in an apartment that feels too quiet without your kids in it. And underneath all the anger at Carol, there's a father who coached baseball and drove Maya to violin lessons — who is genuinely scared of becoming someone his son has to worry about. Tyler asking if you're okay landed hard. Because it meant something was showing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [clears throat] Yeah, that's — that's pretty much it. I think I knew things had gotten out of hand. I just didn't want to say it out loud. Saying it out loud makes it real, you know? But... yeah. That's real.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So if things did start to shift — six months from now — what would you want that to look like for you and your kids?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want Tyler to stop worrying about me. That's the big one. And Maya's got a recital in May — I want to actually be there. Fully there. Not just... showing up. [pause] I think I need to do something different. I don't know what exactly, but — yeah. Something's gotta change. I can see that now.

client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know the last couple of days have been a lot, with everything at the ER. I'm Dr. Reyes — I work here at the VA clinic with folks who are navigating some difficult stuff. How are you feeling right now, just being here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm... okay, I suppose. A little nervous, maybe. I've been to this clinic plenty of times, just never to this kind of appointment. I'm not entirely sure why they sent me here, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It makes sense to feel uncertain. Can you walk me through what happened — what led up to you being in the ER?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I fell. Got dizzy and went down in the kitchen. My daughter found me and she just — she panicked and called 911. I kept telling her I was fine but she wouldn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So from where you were standing, it wasn't as serious as your daughter made it out to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well... I mean, I did hit my head a little. But I've had worse. My hip has been terrible lately and I just — I lost my footing. That's all it was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your hip pain has really been getting to you. Can you tell me more about that — how long you've been dealing with it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh, years. Since my surgery, really. They gave me pills but they only do so much, and I don't like taking too many of them. I don't want to become one of those people who's addicted to their medication. You read about that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're managing something really hard — years of pain — and at the same time you're being careful, thoughtful about not leaning too heavily on the prescription side of things. That takes a kind of discipline.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I try. My husband — he passed six years ago — he always said I was too stubborn for my own good.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'd like to understand what a typical day looks like for you, if that's alright. What does managing the pain look like day to day?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well, I wake up and the first couple hours are the worst. Hip, knees. I take my morning medication — the one they prescribed — and then I just... wait to see what kind of day it's going to be. Some days are better. Some aren't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And where does the alcohol fit into that picture?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I have a glass of wine in the evening. Sometimes two. It helps me relax and... honestly it takes the edge off the pain better than anything else they've given me. I know what the doctors say but it really does help me sleep.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's become a real part of how you get through the hard evenings and nights. What does your family say about it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My daughter doesn't like it. She's been after me about it for... oh, probably a year now. And my son called from Arizona when he heard about the ER and he was very upset. They're making more of it than it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: They're scared for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I know they are. And that's — that's the part that bothers me most, honestly. I don't want them worrying. They have their own lives, their children, their jobs. I shouldn't be... I don't want to be their burden.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That word — burden. Can you say more about what that means to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I raised them, you know? I took care of everything — their father when he was sick, the house, all of it. And now I'm the one they have to check on and lose sleep over? That's not how it's supposed to go. I'm the mother.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've spent your whole life being the one who holds things together. And now you're carrying this — the pain, the nights, the fall — quietly, partly because you love them too much to let it become their problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to bring together what I've heard so far, if that's alright. You've been managing serious chronic pain for years, largely on your own terms. The wine in the evenings has been your way of getting through the hard nights — and it feels like it works better than anything prescribed. You've been careful about not over-relying on medication. And underneath all of it is this strong pull not to worry or burden the people you love. Does that capture it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. That's... yes, that's pretty much it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'd like to share something with you — some information about what happens in the body when alcohol is mixed with certain pain medications. Would that be alright?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The medications you're on for the pain work on the same pathways in the brain and nervous system as alcohol. When they combine, they amplify each other — more than either one would alone. That dizziness before the fall? That's a very common sign of that interaction. It can affect your breathing during sleep, and it makes falls significantly more likely, especially at night. What do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't know it was that... specific. I knew it probably wasn't ideal, mixing them, but I thought it was just like having a drink, same as anyone else would. You're saying the medication changes things.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The medication changes things entirely. And what I'm hearing is that you didn't have the full picture until now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No, I didn't. And if that's what caused the fall... I mean, I live alone. My daughter is forty minutes away. If I had really hurt myself — if I'd hit my head harder or broken my hip — I could have been on that floor for hours.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What comes to mind when you think about what it might look like to manage the pain differently — in a way that didn't carry that kind of risk?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I suppose I'd have to actually talk to my doctor about it. Really talk to her. I've been saying I'm managing fine and I'm... not entirely telling the truth about that. Maybe there's something else they could try. I haven't pushed on it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just named something really important — that you haven't pushed on it, but you could. A lot of people in your situation have accepted the pain as just fixed, as something to quietly endure. You're seeing there might be another path.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've always been good at taking care of other people. I don't think I'm very good at asking for things for myself. That's... that's probably true.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Given everything you've shared today — what feels like one thing you'd be willing to do differently, starting soon?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I should talk to my doctor. Really talk to her — not just say I'm fine. Tell her the nights are hard, tell her what I've been doing to get through them, and see if there's something more we can do. That seems like... the right place to start.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me bring this together before we wrap up. You came in today not entirely sure why you were here. And you're leaving with something concrete: a real conversation with your doctor — one where you tell her the full picture, not just the easy version. And underneath that is something you care about deeply, which is being okay enough that your children don't have to be afraid for you. You've been carrying a lot alone for a long time, and you're starting to see that asking for help isn't the same as becoming a burden.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it that way... yeah. I can do that. It's just a conversation. I've handled harder things than a conversation.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I believe that. Before you go — would you be open to coming back, maybe every few weeks, while you're working through this? You wouldn't have to do it alone.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I would, yes. This was... more helpful than I expected, honestly. Thank you.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again, Harold. You came back — that means something. How are you doing today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well... I said I'd come back, so here I am. Honestly I almost didn't. Sat in the parking lot for about ten minutes. But, uh, I'm here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Ten minutes in the parking lot, and you still walked through that door. What was going through your mind out there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Part of me was thinking, I don't really have a problem, you know? I'm not — I'm not some drunk. But then I thought about what the doctor said, and... I figured I'd come in. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you doesn't feel like this is really a problem. And another part heard something at the doctor's that you couldn't quite shake.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's pretty much it. My liver numbers were — she said they were elevated. Didn't say anything dramatic, but the way she looked at me. Like she was trying not to alarm me but also kind of was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That look from your doctor stuck with you. Tell me a bit about what your drinking has been like since we last talked.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh... about the same. Maybe three, four drinks in the evening. Sometimes I'll have one in the afternoon if — if I'm just sitting there and there's nothing on and I'm... it gets quiet. The house gets really quiet.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The quiet is hard.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It really is. I didn't — I never thought retirement would feel like this. I thought I'd be relieved. Forty years working, you know? But now it's just... I get up and there's nowhere to be. Nobody expecting anything from me. And that's — that's supposed to be the dream, right? But it doesn't feel like a dream.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Forty years of somewhere to be, and now there isn't. That kind of loss — people don't always talk about it, but it's real.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My wife passed four years ago. So it's just me. My kids are... they've got their lives. They call, they do. But it's not — it's not the same as having someone there. And the guys I used to work with, we don't really... we lost touch.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm sorry about your wife. That's a profound loss. When you were still working, what did that give you that you miss now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Structure, I think. And... people. I managed a team — had twelve people under me for the last fifteen years. There was always something. Someone needed something. I felt useful. Now I'm just, uh... I water my plants. Watch the news. I'm useless.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You managed a team for fifteen years. You were someone people counted on. And now you're sitting alone in a quiet house, feeling useless — that's a massive shift in who you are, Harold. No wonder the evenings are hard.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that it sounds... yeah. I hadn't thought of it that way. I just thought I was being weak.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not weak. You're a man who lost his wife, his career, and his community all within a few years. That's a lot to carry. What do you think the drinking is actually doing for you in those quiet moments?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It... takes the edge off. The evenings are the worst. After about six o'clock I just start to feel this — I don't know how to describe it — like a kind of dread. Like the walls are closing in. And having a drink or two, it just... quiets that down. Makes me feel less alone, somehow.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It gives you relief from something that feels almost unbearable. And at the same time, your doctor is telling you it's starting to cost you something physically. How do you sit with both of those things?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Not well. I mean... I'm 65. My father had liver problems. And I saw what that did to him at the end. It wasn't — it wasn't pretty. I don't want that. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You watched your father go through that. You know what that road looks like. And you're saying clearly — you don't want it for yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. No, I don't. I want to... I mean, I've got grandkids. Two of them. Little ones. I want to be around for them. I want to be the kind of grandfather who actually shows up, not just someone they hear about, you know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing from you today. You came back even when part of you wanted to stay in the parking lot — that took something. You've been carrying a lot: losing your wife, leaving your career, feeling cut off from the people you used to know. The drinking helps you get through those long, quiet evenings. And at the same time, your father's experience is sitting in the back of your mind, your doctor is concerned, and you have grandchildren you want to be present for. You're caught between what's getting you through right now and what you actually want your life to look like.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's exactly it. I've never had it laid out like that. It sounds almost obvious when you say it but I haven't — I've been avoiding thinking about it that clearly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean to you to be that grandfather who shows up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Everything. I mean... my granddaughter, she's four. She already runs to me when I come over. I don't want to become someone she's disappointed in. My kids already worry about me. I can see it when they call — they're careful how they word things.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can see the worry in your kids even when they're trying to hide it. Not wanting to disappoint them — that clearly runs deep for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I spent my whole life trying to be reliable. That was my thing. You could count on Harold. And right now I... I'm not sure I could say that about myself. That bothers me more than I let on.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Harold, I want to share something with you, if that's alright. A lot of what you're describing — the dread at six o'clock, the loneliness, using alcohol to manage it — that's a recognized pattern, and it responds well when you address both pieces together. Not just the drinking in isolation, but also the emptiness underneath it. There are real options. You don't have to choose between white-knuckling it alone or just staying where you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't — I honestly thought it was just me being weak or, I don't know, broken. You're saying other people have this? And there's... there's actually something that helps?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There is. And you've already shown you can take hard steps — you came back today. If you were to make one small change this week, something that felt manageable, what might that be?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... I've been thinking about calling my buddy Ray. We worked together for twenty years and I just kind of let that slide. Maybe I call him. And maybe I try skipping that afternoon drink. The evening ones are harder, but the afternoon one — I don't know, maybe I don't actually need that one.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Those are two solid ideas, and they're coming from you. Reconnecting with Ray, cutting the afternoon drink. You're already thinking about this differently than you were in that parking lot.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Ha. Yeah. I guess I am. I mean, I'm not saying it's going to be easy. The evenings are still going to be rough. But I — I'm tired of just... managing. I want to actually feel okay again. Is that possible? At my age?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Absolutely. Age has nothing to do with it. What would feeling okay actually look like for you — what would a good day be?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd get up with somewhere to be. Even something small — a coffee with someone, or maybe volunteering, I don't know. Some reason to get dressed. And in the evening I'd watch TV without needing a drink first to get through it. And maybe call one of my kids just to talk. Not because they're worried about me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Getting up with somewhere to be, evenings you can actually sit through, calling your kids just to connect — that's not out of reach. That's a real life you're describing. And you've mapped a path toward it just in this conversation.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I feel like... I feel a little better than when I came in. Which I wasn't expecting. I thought you'd just tell me to stop drinking and hand me a pamphlet.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No pamphlets today. What I'm hearing is that you came in uncertain, and you're leaving with two concrete things you're actually going to try — calling Ray and skipping that afternoon drink. You know why you want things to be different. You've got grandkids waiting for their grandfather to show up. Let's meet again next week, and I want to hear how both of those went. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I can do that. I'll be here. And I won't sit in the parking lot as long this time.

client_context: A 32-year-old ER nurse who started drinking heavily during the pandemic. Feels guilty but says it's the only way to decompress after traumatic shifts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know the last few weeks have been a lot — finishing detox, and now sitting here. Before we get into anything, I just want to check in. How are you doing right now, in this moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um. Honestly? Tired. I'm just really tired. [pause] I thought I'd feel better after detox. Like, clearer or something. But I mostly just feel... empty. Which sounds dramatic. I'm not trying to be dramatic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't sound dramatic at all. Empty after something that intense — that makes a lot of sense. And tired in a way that goes deeper than just not sleeping.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean — look, I know why I'm here. The labs freaked me out. But I also want to be upfront, I don't think I fit the picture of someone who has a... a 'problem.' I was functioning. I was going to work. I was doing my job. I just needed something to come down after the shifts. It was the only thing that worked.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Those shifts sound like they were a lot to carry. Can you tell me more about what it was like coming home after them?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay, so — you work twelve hours in an ER during a surge and you watch people die alone because no visitors are allowed, and you go home and your head is still there. Still hearing the monitors. You can't sleep, you can't eat, you can't turn it off. And one drink became two and then — [stops] I knew what I was doing. I'm a nurse. I know what the research says. But knowing something and actually caring about it are very different things when you're that exhausted.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were carrying the weight of what you were seeing every day, and at the same time carrying the knowledge of what the drinking was doing. Both at once. That's an enormous amount to hold. [pause] What worries you most when you think about where things were heading?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... [long pause] I made a medication error. About six months ago. I caught it before anything happened, but — I caught it. And I can't prove it was related but I know I wasn't sharp. I was hungover. Not drunk, I would never show up drunk, but not sharp. And that scared me way more than the labs, honestly. Because if something had happened to a patient because of me...

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The thought of something happening to a patient — that landed differently than even the health scare. That one hit the core of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it did. Because... I became a nurse to help people. I know that sounds corny but it's true — I've wanted this since I was like sixteen. And when I realized I was risking that, not just my health but my ability to actually do the job right... something shifted. [quietly] I think that was the moment I actually knew I had to do something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I want to make sure I've got it. You came in because of the lab results — that was the alarm. But the thing that really moved you was that moment with the medication error. Seeing this touch the work, touch the reason you became a nurse in the first place. And even feeling as emptied out as you do right now, some part of you is sitting here to protect that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it like that... yeah. I haven't — I haven't said any of that out loud. My husband knows about the labs but he doesn't know about the error. Nobody does. [pause] I'm still a good nurse. I know I am. I just... I got lost for a while.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You got lost, and you found your way through detox, and now you're here. Looking forward a bit — what does a version of things that actually feels okay look like for you, even just in the next few months?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've actually been thinking about that. Like, during detox I started sleeping — real sleep, not just passing out. And I forgot what that felt like. I want to feel okay when I get home from a shift. Not great, just okay. And I want to trust myself again at work. [small laugh] That would be huge. Just — trusting myself in that room.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Trusting yourself in that room — that goes right to the center of who you are. And you've already done something genuinely hard by getting through detox. The fact that you're here, talking about what it would feel like to actually be okay... that's not nothing. That's a real start.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I — thank you. I'm not used to someone saying that without a 'but' at the end. [pause] I'm not naive, I know this is going to be hard. But I think for the first time in a long time I actually want to try. Not because I'm scared. Because I miss who I was.

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. I want you to know that means something. Last week felt heavy, and you still showed up today. What's been on your mind since we last talked?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I almost didn't. I sat in my car for like... fifteen minutes out there. Almost just drove away. I don't really know why I came in, honestly. Maybe 'cause I paid for it already, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something kept you in that parking lot. And then something got you through that door.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah well. My buddy Dave said I should give it a real shot, not just show up once and bail. Which, for the record, I think is a little rich coming from him, but whatever. Look, I'm here. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Dave sounds like someone who gives a damn about you. And so do you, even if it doesn't feel that way right now. I'm curious — since we last met, what's the week actually looked like for you? Day to day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What's it look like. I go to work. I come home to an apartment I hate. I eat garbage. And yeah, I have a few drinks at night to take the edge off, which I'm sure is what you want to talk about. But that's not — look, the drinking isn't the problem. Karen is the problem. She blew up a twenty-two year marriage because she said she was 'not fulfilled.' Twenty-two years. My kids are at her house and I'm in a one-bedroom in Northbrook.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty-two years. And now you're in a place that doesn't feel like home, without your kids down the hall. That's not a small loss. That's... that's enormous.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's — yeah. It's a lot. But I'm fine. I'm handling it. Men handle things, right? That's what you do. You don't sit around crying about it. You get up, you go to work, you keep moving. The drinks just help me sleep, that's all. It's not like I'm some — I'm not an alcoholic or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't see yourself as someone with a drinking problem. And at the same time... you mentioned a 'wake-up call' when you called to make this appointment. I haven't forgotten that. What happened?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That was — I don't want to make it into a bigger thing than it was. I just... my son called me on a Saturday morning. Ethan. He's sixteen. And I picked up and I was still... I mean I'd had a lot the night before and I was still kind of... foggy. And he wanted to tell me about this thing at school, some project he did, and I couldn't — I kept asking him to repeat himself and he got quiet and then he said 'Dad, are you okay?' And I don't know. Something about that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Ethan's voice on the other end of that phone, asking if you're okay... and something shifted.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't — yeah. I guess. I don't know what it was exactly. I just felt like... like what am I doing? Because he's sixteen and he shouldn't have to be worrying about his dad. He's got enough going on. The divorce hit him hard. He's been quiet ever since.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about Ethan. What's he like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He's a good kid. Really smart. He's into robotics, which, I don't fully get it but he tries to explain it to me and... he used to come into the garage when I was working on the car. Just hang out. Not even talking, just... there. You know? And I miss that. I miss that a lot. Him and his sister both. Sophie's thirteen and she's — she's more like Karen, she processes things, she talks about her feelings. But Ethan just goes quiet and I don't know how to reach him.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You miss just... being in the same space as him. And you're scared you're losing that. Losing the version of you that he could just sit next to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

Yeah. That's — 

I'm sorry. I wasn't expecting that to hit me like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Don't apologize. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... I keep telling myself I'm fine and I'm holding it together but I think... I think I'm scared that if I stop drinking I'll have to actually feel all of it. And I don't know if I can. I haven't cried. Not once in four months. Not even at the — when I had to tell my parents. I just sat there and explained it like it was happening to someone else.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The drinking has been keeping that door shut. And part of you knows it, and part of you is terrified of what's on the other side of that door.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... yeah. I think that's right. And the thing is, I'm not stupid. I know what I'm doing. I know it's not — the amount I'm drinking, it's not good. Most nights it's like half a bottle of scotch, sometimes more. That's not nothing. I know that. I just didn't want to say it out loud I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect something back to you, because I think you've said something really important today. You came back even though you almost didn't. You told me about Ethan and that Saturday morning phone call. You named what the drinking is actually doing — not sleeping, not coping, but keeping the grief locked up. And you just said out loud, maybe for the first time, that it's not good. That takes something. That takes courage, even if it doesn't feel that way.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't feel particularly courageous. I feel like a fifty-year-old man sitting in a therapist's office crying about his ex-wife. But I don't know. Maybe that's... maybe that's something. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If things were different — even a little different — what would that look like for you? Not perfect, just... different.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd be... I don't know, present I guess? Like when Ethan calls I'd actually be there. And maybe I'd get my own place that doesn't feel like a hotel room. Put some of my stuff in it. And I'd like to — I keep thinking about this fishing trip I promised him before everything fell apart. Up in Wisconsin. I never took him. And I think about that a lot actually.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That fishing trip hasn't gone anywhere. Ethan's still sixteen. And you're still his dad.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's true. He is. And I think — I actually think if I called him this week and said 'let's plan that trip,' he'd say yes. He'd want to. Because underneath all of it, we're still us, you know? That doesn't just disappear.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would need to be different for you to make that call — and actually show up for that trip?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd need to — I'd have to get the drinking under control. I can't take him on a fishing weekend and be... I can't do that to him. So I'd need to deal with that. And I think I need to — I don't know, maybe talk to my doctor. I haven't told him any of this either. I've been telling everyone I'm fine for four months and I'm just... I'm tired of doing that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You walked in here today not sure why you came. And you're leaving with something you didn't have when you walked in — you know what you're actually carrying, you know why it matters, and you know the next step. Talking to your doctor. That's real. That's a real thing you can do this week. I'll be here when you come back.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. I'll... yeah, I'll call him. I think I can do that. And I'll come back. I think I actually want to, which is — that's not something I would've said walking in here today.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, Marcus. Come on in. I noticed you walked in a little differently today. Last week was already hard, and... I'm just glad you're here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah well. Not like I had a choice, right? Judge says come or I go back in. So here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're here because the court's making you, and that doesn't feel right.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Doesn't feel right? It IS wrong. I had two beers. Two. And they want me sitting here every week talking about my feelings like I'm some kind of... I don't know. It's a waste of my time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And on top of all that — you mentioned last week things were going to be rough. What happened this week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What happened? What happened is I lost my overtime. Boss says I can't drive the company van anymore because of the license suspension. So now I'm taking the bus like — twenty-three years I've worked there. Twenty-three years. And now I'm some kind of liability.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty-three years of showing up, and now they're treating you like you don't matter. That's... that's a real gut punch.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's bullshit. Excuse my language. But it is. And everyone just acts like I deserve it. My brother, my ex, the judge — like I'm some drunk in a gutter. I had two beers at a cookout. This whole thing is — it's not fair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: ... You're carrying a lot right now. The job, your brother, your ex. And underneath all the anger, I'm hearing someone who doesn't feel seen. Who feels like the people around him have already made up their minds about who he is.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah well. Maybe they have. ... [pause] The thing is — look, I'm not gonna sit here and cry about it. I just — I don't see the point. Nothing I do changes what they think.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to ask you about something else, if that's okay. The letter from your doctor — the lab results. You brought it up at the end of last session and then kind of... changed the subject pretty quick.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Um. I got a call. Liver enzymes or something. The numbers were elevated. Whatever that means.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not entirely sure what it means. And maybe part of you doesn't want to know.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — I'm not some hypochondriac. Doctor said it could be a lot of things. Stress, diet, whatever. He didn't say it was definitely anything serious. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What did he say he wanted to do next?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: More tests. Follow-up bloodwork. He was... he was kind of serious about it, actually. Like his face — he wasn't joking around. But he said we'd know more in a few weeks.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: His face told you something his words maybe didn't. And you've been sitting with that ever since.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I didn't — I haven't really talked about it. Didn't tell my kids. They don't need that. But yeah, it's been... it's just there. Every morning I wake up and it's right there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying that completely alone. And still walking through that door every week. That takes something, Marcus. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't know. I just — [pause] — I've got two kids. Fourteen and eleven. Their mom and I aren't together anymore but I'm still their dad. And I keep thinking... what if this is actually something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does being their dad mean to you? Like, what do you want that to look like — for them?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want — [long pause] — I want to be there. Not just physically there but... my old man was around but he wasn't really around, you know what I'm saying? He was checked out. Drinking, mostly. And I swore I wasn't gonna be him. I swore that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You made yourself a promise — I am not going to be my father. And right now, some part of you is wondering if you've kept it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... [very long pause] ... Yeah. I guess I am. I'm not — I want to be clear, I'm not like him. I'm not. But um... I don't know. Maybe I've let some things get out of hand. I'm not saying the DUI was — I still think that whole thing was unfair. But, uh... maybe I've been drinking more than I should. Just to, like... take the edge off.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to hold all of this together for a second. You came in today angry — and honestly, with real reasons to be. You lost income, you feel like everyone around you has already written you off, and the system doesn't feel fair. Underneath that, there's a letter from a doctor you've been carrying alone for weeks. And then there's this quieter thing — this fear that maybe you're becoming someone you promised yourself you'd never be. And your kids are right there in the center of all of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. That's — yeah. That's kind of it, actually. [exhales slowly] I didn't expect to say any of that out loud today.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said 'maybe I've let some things get out of hand.' What would it look like — to you — if you decided to actually do something about that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm not gonna commit to anything right now. I want to be straight about that. But, um... maybe actually go back to the doctor. Like, really hear what he says instead of just hoping it goes away. And maybe... I don't know. Cut back some. See what that even feels like.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not making a big declaration. But you're thinking about going back to the doctor — really listening this time — and curious what it'd feel like to ease off. That's a different place than where you walked in today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. Don't read too much into it. [pause] But... yeah. Maybe. I'm just tired. I'm really, really tired.

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for getting on today, Marcus. I know this isn't exactly how you planned to spend your Tuesday. I'd like to just start by hearing from you — what's been going on in your life lately?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... the court thing, right? That's why I'm here. I got a DUI, I know that. Look, I'm not — I don't think I'm some kind of alcoholic or whatever. It was one bad night. I just need to do the hours and be done with it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: One bad night that ended up here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... it's been a rough few months, I'll give you that. The divorce was finalized in December and things just kind of... fell apart after that. But that doesn't mean I have a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about that — what has 'fell apart' looked like for you since December?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't... I mean, 22 years. We were married 22 years and she just — I came home one day and she said she was done. And my kids, I see them every other weekend now. Every other weekend. Like I'm some kind of... visitor in my own family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You went from being there every single day to every other weekend. That's not a small thing. That's a massive loss.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is. And nobody — nobody really talks about how that just... it wrecks you. You're supposed to keep going to work and be fine. I started having a drink at night. Just to sleep. To stop the thoughts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What were those nights like, when you couldn't sleep?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Dark. Just dark. I'm renting now — renting, at 48 — and I'd sit in that apartment and just think about everything. What I did wrong, what she did, whether my kids think I abandoned them. A few drinks takes the edge off. Doesn't fix anything but at least you can breathe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It gave you some relief from thoughts that were pretty overwhelming.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. And look, I know it's not... I know it's not a great solution. I'm not stupid. But what else am I supposed to do? I can't call my ex. My friends — half of them took her side or just disappeared. I got nothing going on at night.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So in the span of four months you lost your marriage, your daily life with your kids, your home, and most of your social network — all at once. And alcohol has been basically the only thing giving you any relief from all of that. That's not 'a rough few months.' That's a lot of loss stacked on top of loss.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you say it like that... yeah. Yeah, that's it. I keep waiting for it to get better and it just... hasn't. I don't know if it's going to, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you has started wondering if it ever will.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My son — he's 15 — he called me last week and I could tell I woke him up. It was 11 on a Tuesday. I didn't realize. I just missed him and I wasn't... I wasn't drunk but I'd had a few and he was half asleep and I just... I felt like a complete piece of shit after.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That call stayed with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He didn't say anything about it. He's a good kid, he was nice. But I know he noticed — he's sharp. And I keep thinking I don't want him to remember me like this. At 48, calling him at 11pm from some shitty apartment. That's not... that's not who I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That says something real — you still know who you are, and this isn't it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I was always the one who showed up, you know? Coached his little league, never missed a recital. Now I'm the guy who... I don't recognize myself. I look in the mirror and I don't know who that is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean to you to be that father again — the one who showed up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Everything. Honestly, that's... he's the reason I even got on this call today. Not the court order. I figured, you know, maybe I need to just hear what someone has to say. Because what I'm doing is clearly not working.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came here for him. Not because you had to.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And for me too, I guess. I'm just... I'm tired. Tired of the anger, tired of — I miss her too, which makes me angrier, which is stupid. I don't want to feel like this every day. I want to feel like myself again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing. You came in today thinking this was just about checking a box for court. But what you've actually told me is that you're exhausted by the grief and the anger, that you miss being the father you were, and that you want to feel like yourself again. That's not nothing — that's a real reason to do something different.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've never said any of that out loud before. My buddy just keeps telling me to man up and I just... this is the first time talking about it hasn't felt like getting punched in the face.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Given everything you've said — your son, being exhausted, wanting to feel like yourself — what's one thing, even a small thing, you might be willing to try?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've been thinking about... there's an AA meeting near my apartment. I've driven past it a few times. I always thought it wasn't for me but maybe... maybe I just go once and see. And I keep bourbon in the cabinet and if it's not there I can't drink it at midnight, right? So maybe I stop buying it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've already been thinking about this. You drove past that meeting more than once. Those aren't small steps, Marcus — that's you starting to choose your son, and yourself, over what's been getting you through the night. That took something to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't feel courageous. I feel like I wasted four months. But... yeah. Maybe it's not too late.

client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thank you for coming in today. I know this isn't easy, especially right after finishing the program. Before we get into anything, I just want to ask — what's on your mind as you sit here right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I don't really know where to start, honestly. I'm still trying to make sense of everything. The past few weeks have been... a lot. I didn't sleep well last night. I keep going over things in my head.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A lot to take in. [pause] You said you keep going over things — what part feels hardest to make sense of?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well... I mean, I never thought of myself as someone with a drinking problem. I just — the pain was so bad some nights. The doctors, they could only do so much. A glass of wine helped me sleep. That's all I thought it was. That's what I told myself, anyway.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So for you, the drinking wasn't reckless. It was you trying to cope with something very real — the pain, the sleeplessness. A way of getting through the night.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. I mean... well. Maybe I let it go further than I should have. I can see that now. But at the time I just — I didn't see another way. And I'm 72. I suppose some part of me thought, does it even matter that much anymore?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: And yet here you are. That tells me something — that some part of you decided it does still matter. That took real courage.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I don't know if it was courage so much as — George said he'd leave. My husband. And that... that frightened me more than anything. I can't bear the thought of being alone. Not now. Not at this age.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about that. What would it mean to you — losing George?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: We've been married 48 years. Forty-eight. He's... he's why I get up in the morning. And to see the look on his face these past months — that fear, that exhaustion — I did that. I put that there. That is not who I am. It's not who I ever wanted to be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You feel responsible for his pain. And that's not sitting well with you at all.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. It's not. I... [long pause] I'm ashamed. I really am. My daughter had to drive me to the hospital. And my granddaughter — she's only nine — she saw me like that. I just keep thinking about the look on her face. I can't get it out of my head.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was it like for you — being seen that way by the people you love most?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Awful. Just... awful. I've spent my whole life trying not to be a burden to anyone. I raised three children mostly on my own before George came along. I've always been the one who holds everything together. And now I'm the one falling apart. It's humiliating.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been strong for so many people for so many years. And somewhere along the way, the pain — the physical pain — just became too much to carry quietly on your own.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. [quietly] That's it exactly. I never told anyone how bad it really got. I didn't want to worry them. So I just... handled it. Mostly at night. A glass or two to take the edge off. And then it became more. I don't even know when that happened.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what you've shared, if that's all right. You've been living with serious chronic pain and managing it in silence, not wanting to worry your family. The drinking started as a way to cope — with the pain, the sleeplessness. Over time it grew into something that harmed your health and frightened the people closest to you. You're here because you don't want to lose George, and because something in you recognizes this isn't the person you want to be. Is that close to how you'd describe it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yes. That's right. [pause] When you say it like that it sounds so clear. I couldn't have put it that way myself. It's been all jumbled up in my head, going round and round.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Now that it feels a little clearer — what matters most to you, going forward from here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to be present. Really present. Not foggy, not... not like I was. George deserves that. And I want to be around for my grandchildren — truly around. I want to see them grow up with a grandmother who's actually there, you know? Not just in the room, but... there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being fully present — for George, for your grandchildren. That's what you're reaching toward.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Mm. And... I think I want to feel like myself again. I lost myself somewhere in all of it. The pain, the medication, the wine... I used to do the crossword every morning. I used to garden. I haven't touched my garden in over a year. That's not me. That's not who I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned you've always been someone who holds things together. Raising children on your own, managing years of pain, getting through detox — what strengths do you think you have that you can lean on now, going forward?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Hmm. I hadn't thought about it like that. [pause] I suppose... I'm stubborn. In a good way, I hope. And I do care deeply about people. Maybe too deeply sometimes. But I don't give up easily. I mean — I'm here, aren't I? That's something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You are here. And I want to name that — completing detox at this stage in life, with the health challenges you're carrying, is genuinely hard. You did that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I did, didn't I. [small laugh] George cried when they discharged me. Big ugly cry, right there in the parking lot. That man... [pause] I want to make him proud. I want to make myself proud. I think that's the first time I've said that out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
