utterances.text: What would a first step look like for you — something small but real that moves you in that direction?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... talking to my doctor honestly this time. About how bad the pain has really been. I've been downplaying it for years. Maybe there are other options I never asked about. And coming back here. Talking to you. I think that would help. I really do.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So to bring our time together to a close today — you came in here carrying a lot of shame and confusion, but also a real desire to find your way back to yourself. You care deeply about George and your grandchildren. You have a stubbornness and a strength that have carried you through hard things before. Your next steps are to have an honest conversation with your doctor about pain management, and to continue here in counseling. That sounds like a solid foundation to me. I'm genuinely glad you came today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: So am I. I was terrified walking through that door, if I'm honest. But I feel... lighter. A little bit. Like maybe there's a way through this after all.

client_context: A 55-year-old who lost their spouse 8 months ago and has been drinking to numb the pain. Isolated from friends and family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come in, Eleanor. Good to see you made it today. You mentioned when you called that this past week was rough — I want to make sure we have space for that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I'm here. I almost didn't come, honestly. I just... I don't know, I almost cancelled. But I figured you'd want to know how it went.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm glad you came. Tell me what happened this week — in your own words, whatever feels important.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want you to make it into a bigger thing than it is. I had a rough night, I drank more than I — more than planned, okay? But it was one night. It's not like it's a pattern or — I mean, it's not like every night is like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something about that night was different from the others.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — yes. But I can usually manage fine. I'm not... look, I'm not some kind of alcoholic sitting in a ditch somewhere. I held a job for thirty-two years. I raised a daughter. I know how to hold myself together.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I hear you — that's not how you see yourself. So what was it about that particular night that made it harder to hold yourself together?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... God, this is going to sound stupid. It was Richard's birthday. I woke up and for like — maybe two seconds — I forgot. My brain just... and then it hit me again. All at once. And the whole day just kind of collapsed after that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: For a moment, he was still here. And then you had to lose him all over again.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, that's — that's exactly what it feels like. Every time. Like it just resets and I have to start from zero. It never gets... sorry. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Don't apologize. That's a brutal kind of pain. I want to ask you something honest — what did drinking do for you that night? What did it give you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It... it quieted everything down. Is that awful? I know how that sounds. But for a few hours I just — I wasn't drowning. The noise in my head just stopped. I'm not proud of it, but I'm not going to lie to you about it either.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It worked. It gave you relief from something that felt completely unbearable. And I'm also hearing something underneath that — like you're not entirely okay with the way you got there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not. I woke up the next morning and I just felt... ashamed. Like, genuinely ashamed of myself. Richard would have hated seeing me like that. He was the strong one in this marriage. He never — he would have hated it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The fact that you felt that — the shame, the awareness of it — that's not you falling apart. That's you still knowing what matters to you, even in the middle of all this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I used to be strong too. I really was. People used to come to me with their problems. I was the one who held things together. And now I just... I don't know where that woman went.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Where do you think she went?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She went with him, I think. I stopped calling my daughter as much. I quit book club — just made excuses until they stopped asking. I used to go to church every Sunday and now I... I haven't been in six months. Most nights it's just me and a bottle of wine and whatever's on TV. And I know — I know that's not living. I know that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can see the distance between the life you're living right now and the life you want to be living. And that gap — it hurts.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It really does. I keep telling myself the drinking is just... getting me through. But through to what? It's been eight months. At some point, is this just... is this who I am now? Is this giving up?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a real question — getting through to what. What do you think Richard would say if you asked him that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He'd say... *laughs softly* he'd say 'Eleanor, you've got too much life left to waste it sitting in that house.' That sounds like a greeting card. But that's him. He was always dragging me out of my comfort zone. He never let me shrink. And I've been... I've been shrinking for eight months.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been shrinking. And some part of you is really tired of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I am. I am so tired of being sad and small. I'm fifty-five years old. That's not old. My mother lived to eighty-nine. I could have thirty more years and I'm spending them... like this. It's not what I want. It's not what either of us would have wanted.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing. You had a terrible night — Richard's birthday, that grief hitting you fresh all over again — and the drinking got you through it. But you woke up ashamed. You can see that you've pulled away from your daughter, your friends, everything that used to be yours. And underneath all of that, there's still a woman who knows she has more life ahead of her. Someone who doesn't want to keep shrinking.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's — when you put it that way, that's all true. Every bit of that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So if you were going to take one small step this week — not a total overhaul, just one thing — what might that look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've been thinking about calling my daughter. Sarah. We used to talk every Sunday without fail and now it's... maybe once a month, and even then it's short. I've been avoiding it because she sounds like him sometimes, the way she laughs. But I think — I'm going to call her. This Sunday. Actually call, not just text.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That takes real courage — reaching toward someone when everything in you has been pulling away. Calling Sarah this Sunday matters more than you might realize right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think so too. I hope so. Yeah... I'm going to try.

client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hello, Margaret. I'm glad you came in today. I know the past week has been a lot — finishing detox is no small thing. I'd like for us to take this time at whatever pace feels right for you. There's no agenda we have to rush through. So... how are you feeling right now, in this moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm... tired, mostly. Just very tired. I didn't sleep well at the facility. I kept thinking I shouldn't be there, you know? Like, I'm seventy-two years old and I'm in a detox program. That's not... that's not who I thought I was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like being there brought up a lot of feelings about your sense of self — who you are, who you've always seen yourself as. What was that week like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Humbling. That's the word. I raised three children on my own after my husband passed. I worked as a nurse for thirty-one years. And then my back gave out, and the hip, and the pain was just so constant... and the wine helped me sleep. And then it was wine and the pills, and I didn't even notice how much until my daughter found me on the kitchen floor one morning and she was — she was screaming, and I... I don't want to think about her face.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your daughter's face that morning — that image is still with you. And underneath everything you've shared, I'm hearing someone who spent her whole life taking care of others, and who is now grappling with what it means to need care herself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's exactly it. I don't want to be a burden. I never wanted that. My kids have their own lives, their jobs, the grandchildren — they don't need to be worrying about me on top of everything else. And now my son calls me every single day, twice sometimes, and I can hear how scared he is, and I just... I feel so guilty. I don't know how to fix that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You completed an entire week of detox — that is not a small thing, and it took real courage. The fact that you're here, in this chair, after everything your body has been through and everything your heart has been carrying... that says something important about who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... thank you. I don't feel courageous. I feel like I made a terrible mess. But I do want to fix it. I really do. I just — I don't know if I can manage the pain without something. That's what scares me. The pain doesn't go away just because I stopped drinking.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really honest and important thing to name — the pain is real and it hasn't gone anywhere, and we'll need to address that together. But I'm also curious: when you say you want to fix this... what does that look like to you? What would your life be like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to be... present. For my grandchildren. There's a little one, she's four, and she calls me Nana Maggie and she likes to sit in my lap and have me read to her. And lately I've been so foggy, or in pain, or just... not really there. I want to be there for her. I want her to have a grandmother she can actually remember.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being present for her — that's at the center of this for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She is. She really is. And I think... for the first time in a long time, I can see why it matters. Why I matter. Does that sound strange? I've been taking care of everyone else for so long, it's like I forgot that I'm — that I'm a person too. That I'm worth... worth taking care of.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I've heard today, and you tell me if I'm getting it right. You came through a detox program this past week — something you never imagined for yourself — and it shook your sense of who you are. You've spent your life as a caregiver, a nurse, a mother, and you've been living with chronic pain that has been very real and very hard to manage. You started using alcohol to cope with that pain, and it escalated in a way that frightened your family and frightened you. And underneath the guilt and the exhaustion, there is something very clear: a four-year-old who calls you Nana Maggie, and the version of yourself you want to be for her. And today, you said something remarkable — that you are worth taking care of too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yes. That's it. That's all of it. I told myself I wasn't going to cry today. But yes — that's exactly right.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've given us a really strong foundation to build on. As we think about moving forward — managing the pain more safely, staying connected with your family, being present for your granddaughter — what feels like one step you'd be willing to take between now and when we meet again?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I want to call my daughter. Not to apologize again — I've done that enough, I think. Just to talk. Maybe ask if I can come see the little one this weekend. Just to sit with her. I think that would help me more than anything.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I'm Marcus. Take a seat wherever feels right — that chair, the couch, the floor if you're feeling adventurous. So, what brings you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What brings me in? Are you serious right now? The court brings me in. My lawyer brings me in. I don't actually — I mean, this is the last place I want to be on a Tuesday afternoon, man. I got stuff to do. I got a job. And instead I'm sitting here because apparently I need to talk to somebody about my — quote unquote — drinking problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah, that tracks. Being told where to be and when to be there — especially somewhere like this — that would put anyone on edge. You didn't exactly choose to walk through that door.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And everyone keeps acting like I'm some kind of... I don't know, like I'm a drunk who can't function or something. I go to work every day. I pay my bills. I'm not sitting under a bridge somewhere. But one night — one night things go sideways and suddenly I'm the problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's this gap between how you see yourself and how the system is framing you right now. I'm curious — what actually happened that night? I mean, from your perspective.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I had a few beers at my buddy's watching the game. Few beers. I wasn't blackout, I wasn't swerving all over the road. Cop pulls me over for a taillight — a taillight — and breathalyzer says point-one-two. So yeah, okay, technically over the limit, fine. But this is my second one and they're treating me like I'm some kind of menace. It's the system just piling on, man. That's all it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is saying point-one-two, a few beers, the situation felt manageable — and at the same time, this is the second time you've ended up here. That second part's gotta be sitting with you a little.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah it does. I thought after the first one I'd just be more careful, you know? Watch it. And here I am. And my daughter — she's twelve — she found out and she didn't talk to me for like a week. That was... that was rough. That one got to me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your daughter not talking to you — that hit different than the legal stuff. Tell me more about what that was like.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She's... I mean, she's everything, right? She's the reason I get up. And she looked at me like — I don't even know how to describe it — like she was scared of me or embarrassed or something. And I keep thinking, what am I teaching her? What does she think her dad is? That stuff... I don't sit with that real easily.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being a dad she can look up to — that really matters to you. And somewhere underneath all the frustration about the court and the system, you're asking yourself if you're actually living up to that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I am. I don't want her to grow up thinking that's just... that's what men do, you know? That's not who I want to be. I always figured I had it handled. Maybe I don't have it as handled as I thought. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me see if I'm tracking you right. You came in here pretty fired up — the court, the system, feeling like this whole thing was overblown. And that's still part of it. But there's also something else sitting underneath that: a second DUI, your daughter shutting down on you for a week, and a quiet question starting to form about whether drinking is actually working the way you want it to. Those two things seem to be living side by side right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... That's pretty accurate, yeah. I didn't come in here thinking I'd be saying any of this. Thought I'd just sit here, do my time, and leave. But... I don't know. Maybe there's something worth looking at. I'm not saying I'm an alcoholic or whatever. But. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: "Maybe" is actually a pretty big word — especially coming from someone who walked in ready to count ceiling tiles for an hour. So if you were going to look at something — just one thing — what would you want to understand better about your relationship with drinking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I'd want to understand why I always go one more than I planned to. Like I tell myself two beers, and it's never two. It's never two. And I don't totally get that about myself. I'd... I'd like to.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know walking into a place like this isn't always easy. Can you tell me a little about what brings you here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh... I mean, my wife basically gave me an ultimatum. Come here or she's done. So. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're here partly because of what's happening at home. There's a lot riding on this for you right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I guess. Look, I'm not — I don't think I'm some kind of alcoholic, okay? I'm a bartender. Drinking's just... it's part of the culture. Everyone I work with does it. It's not like I'm hiding bottles under the sink or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does a typical night look like for you after a shift?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I get home at like 2, 3 in the morning. I'm wired, I can't just... sleep. A few drinks takes the edge off. Always has. I don't even really think about it anymore, it's just — it's routine. Wind down, go to bed. Normal stuff.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You just got through a week of detox. That's not nothing — that actually takes a real kind of commitment, especially when you're not even sure you need it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: The detox was... I mean, it sucked. I didn't want to be there. The first two days I was sick as hell and I'm just lying there thinking, this is insane, I am not that bad. People in there had real problems.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What happened toward the end of the week — the last few days in there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... weird. I started actually sleeping. Like, real sleep. And I woke up one morning and I realized — I can't remember the last time I woke up without a headache. Not a hangover, just like, a regular headache. Every morning. I just thought that was normal. That kind of... I don't know what to do with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something shifted in that quiet. You noticed something about yourself you hadn't expected to find.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I started doing the math in my head. Like, when was the last sober day? And I couldn't — I genuinely could not name one. Not one. That kind of freaked me out, honestly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me make sure I'm tracking this right. You came today because Lena asked you to, and part of you is still not convinced there's a real problem. But then you went through detox — which was rough — and something unexpected happened: you slept well, the headaches lifted, and when you tried to find the last day you hadn't drunk, you couldn't. And that scared you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. That's pretty much it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does it mean to you — that you couldn't find that day?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... okay, my dad drank. A lot. And I always swore I wasn't gonna be that guy. And I wasn't — I held down a job, I showed up, I'm not him. But Lena keeps saying I'm not really there even when I'm there. And sitting in that room for a week I think I started to... I get what she means now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You built a lot of your identity around not being your father. And now there's a part of you wondering if the distance between you and him is smaller than you thought.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's — I don't like thinking about it that way, but... yeah. Like, I'll be standing behind the bar and I'm already thinking about when I get to have mine. I didn't used to be like that. That's not — that's not who I was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're able to see that in yourself. A lot of people can't — or won't. That takes honesty.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't know if it's honesty or if everything just kind of piled up at once. Lena crying, the detox, a week with nothing to do but stare at the ceiling. I kind of had no choice but to look at it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you imagine things actually being different — what does that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to come home and actually be... present. Not just a body on the couch. I want Lena to look at me the way she used to. And I think — I think I want to know what I'm actually like without it. Because honestly? I'm not even sure anymore. I've been doing this since I was like nineteen.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You want to find out who you are on the other side of this. And you want your marriage back.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Both those things. I just... I don't know how to do the job and not drink. That's the part that terrifies me. Like what do I do at 2am when every single person around me is drinking and that's just the air I breathe?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's a real tension there — you can see what you want, you can feel it pulling at you, and at the same time there's genuine fear about what it actually costs to get there given where you work, who you are. Those two things can both be true at once.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It's like... I want to change but I don't know how to change and still be me. Or like — what's even left of me if I take that part out. Does that make any sense?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It makes a lot of sense. What feels like the most important next step — just from where you're sitting right now, today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Coming back here. I think I need to keep talking to someone because if I'm on my own I will rationalize it into nothing. I know I will. I'm really good at that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know yourself well enough to name that — and you're choosing to do something about it anyway. That matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want to be the guy who loses everything and then figures it out. I want to... I don't know. Maybe be smarter than that for once. We'll see.

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in, Marcus. I know walking into a new place like this isn't always easy. I'm going to skip the formal intake checklist for now — I'd rather just hear from you directly. How are you doing today, just to start?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh... yeah. I'm, um... I'm here. That's about the best I can say right now. Honestly I wasn't sure I was gonna walk through that door this morning.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What made you come in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My buddy Dave — he kind of... he sat me down last week. Said I'd changed. That I wasn't myself anymore. That was, uh... that hit different coming from him. We've known each other twenty-some years. I figured, okay, maybe I should at least talk to someone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something about hearing it from Dave got through in a way other things haven't. Tell me a little more about what he said — what did he actually notice?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He said I was... withdrawn. Like, showing up to things but not really there. Look, I've done the whole counseling thing before, and it never really... it doesn't usually do much for me. No offense.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No offense taken — and I appreciate you being straight with me. That's useful to know. I'm not going to try to convince you this will be different. Tell me what the drinking has been like these past few months.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... look, it's not like I'm drinking in the morning or whatever. I come home after work, I have a few beers, maybe some whiskey on the weekends. It's how I unwind. After everything that's happened this year... I think I've earned a little unwinding.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The drinking has been how you've gotten through it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And honestly? Sandra — my ex — she would've found something else to complain about even if I quit tomorrow. It wasn't just the drinking. She just... decided she was done. Four months ago. Boom. Done.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds like it came out of nowhere for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She packed up the kids and went to her mother's. My kids are there now. I'm in that house by myself, and I don't even know what to do with myself when I come home. There's nobody there. So yeah. I drink.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The house is empty. The kids aren't there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. [long pause] ...Danny's nine. Lily's six. I get them on weekends, when Sandra lets me, which isn't always. And I just... I don't know. That part's different. That part's harder than I thought it'd be.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's it like walking into that house when they're not there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... [exhales slowly] it's quiet. Like, a kind of quiet that's not normal. I still have their drawings on the fridge. Haven't taken them down. I don't... I can't explain why. I just can't do it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're holding on to them.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm a mess. I know that. I thought I was just angry, you know? For weeks it was just rage. At Sandra, at everything. And now it's like the anger is still there but underneath it there's... I don't know what to call it. This is something else.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to put together what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I've got it right. You came in because someone who knows you well said you'd changed. You've been drinking more — in your mind it's the thing keeping you going since everything fell apart. And underneath the anger, which has been real, there's something that feels more like grief. Missing your kids, missing the life you had. You're not sure counseling can help, but some part of you showed up today anyway.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. That's, uh... yeah. [quiet] I haven't really said all of that out loud before. Not like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If the drinking wasn't in the picture the way it is now — what would be different for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd probably... actually deal with stuff, I guess. Instead of just numbing it every night. And when Danny and Lily are with me, I'd be more... present. Last weekend Danny asked me something and I just — I wasn't really there. I hate that. I hate that I did that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Being present for them — that matters to you more than almost anything else you've said today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: They're everything. They're the whole reason... [pauses] Look, they're why I came in, if I'm honest. Not Dave. Not Sandra. Them. I don't want them to look back and remember their dad as someone who just... wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So thinking about just the next week or two — what would one small step look like that moves you toward being the dad you want to be?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I could... the nights before I have them, keep those clear. No drinking. At least that. It's not like fixing everything but it's... I've got to start somewhere, right? Start with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came in here today not sure any of this would go anywhere. You said things out loud you hadn't let yourself say before. And you just named exactly what matters most to you and something real you're willing to do about it. That's not nothing, Marcus.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't feel like it's brave or whatever. I feel like I should've done this months ago. But... thank you. That actually means something to hear.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Here's where we are. You came in guarded — you've been through this before and it hasn't stuck. But today you told me about Danny and Lily, about the quiet house, about what you're actually carrying under all that anger. And you landed on something concrete: keeping the nights before you see them clear. That's a real place to start. I'd like to keep meeting with you if you're open to it. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I want to keep coming back. I actually do. [small laugh] That's, uh... that's new for me.

client_context: A 24-year-old PhD student who has been drinking to manage thesis stress and imposter syndrome. Advisor noticed declining work quality.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in. I know you said you were between classes so I appreciate you making the time. No rush, we'll go at whatever pace works for you today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, um... thanks. Sorry, I just — I walked here from the chem building so I'm kind of... yeah. I'm here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You made it. That counts for something. So — what's going on for you? What made today the day to come in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh... I mean, the ER thing. My roommate kind of... insisted. I don't think it was as bad as it looked, honestly. I just hadn't eaten and I had a few drinks and my blood pressure was weird or whatever. It wasn't like a — I wasn't trying to hurt myself or anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So in your mind, it was kind of a perfect storm — empty stomach, some drinks, your body just reacted. And you want me to know it wasn't intentional.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. Yeah. Exactly. I just... I've been really stressed and I wasn't being careful and it got out of hand. That's all it was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me a little more about the drinking lately. What does a typical week look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it depends. When things are okay, like maybe a few beers on the weekend. But the last couple months with the thesis... I don't know, it kind of crept up. Like I'd have something at night just to — to turn my brain off. And then it became kind of a thing where I couldn't really fall asleep without it. Which sounds worse than it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like it started as a way to get some relief — to just quiet things down at the end of the day — and then somewhere along the way, your body started to depend on it to sleep.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's actually pretty accurate. And that kind of freaks me out, honestly. Because I didn't — I mean, I'm not someone who has a drinking problem. That's not who I am. So when I notice that I'm like... reaching for it before I even think about it, that's...

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What goes through your head in those moments — when you notice yourself reaching for it without even thinking?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Sometimes nothing. That's the scary part. It's just — it's automatic. And then afterward I'm like, okay, how many is that tonight? And the number is higher than I thought it was. And I'm sitting there at my desk at like 1am having accomplished nothing and I just feel... terrible. Like what am I doing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The fact that you're paying attention to that — noticing the number, asking yourself what you're doing — that's not nothing. A lot of people go a long time without letting themselves see it that clearly.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess. I mean I didn't have much of a choice after the ER thing. My roommate was pretty shaken up. And my advisor emailed me. Which is — god, that was humiliating.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What did your advisor say?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She was... actually really kind about it, which somehow made it worse? She said she'd noticed my work had been slipping and she was worried about me, and she asked if I needed to take a leave or something. And I just — I sat there reading it thinking, she's right. She's right and I've been telling myself she doesn't notice, but she does. Everyone probably does.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something about her noticing — and being kind about it — really landed for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because I can handle it when people are frustrated with me. I've been handling my parents being disappointed my whole life, whatever. But when someone's just... worried? That's different. That means something's actually wrong. Like actually wrong, not me-being-dramatic wrong.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just make sure I'm understanding everything you've shared. You came in after an ER visit that scared your roommate and, honestly, scared a part of you too. You've been drinking more than usual — it started as a way to manage thesis stress and shut your brain down at night, but it's gotten to the point where it feels automatic, and the numbers are higher than you'd like. You noticed your work is slipping, your advisor noticed, and when she reached out with concern rather than frustration, it hit you differently — like this is real. Does that capture it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... it. That's the whole thing laid out like that and it sounds pretty bad when you say it all together.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came to this program because something mattered enough to fight for a PhD. What was that? What were you after when you started?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... okay, this is going to sound naive. But I genuinely thought I could do research that mattered. Like, I grew up in a pretty rural area and there were people around me who had real health problems and no resources, and I thought — if I can figure something out at the molecular level, maybe that helps someone eventually. I know that's like a ten-year pipeline at minimum but that was the thing. That was why.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not naive at all. And here's what I notice — the guy who wanted to do that work? He's still in there. He's sitting in front of me right now. But it sounds like somewhere along the way, the drinking started taking up the space where that drive used to live.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... yeah. That's exactly what happened. I don't even know when. I think the imposter syndrome just got so loud that the drinking became like — noise canceling headphones? And I just kept turning the volume up and at some point I forgot to actually do the work.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Noise-canceling headphones. That's actually a really sharp way to describe it. You found something that worked in the short run — and you used it because the alternative, sitting with all that doubt and pressure, felt unbearable.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. And it's not like I'm weak, I just — I didn't have another way to deal with it. But I'm also starting to see that the headphones are broken, you know? Like they don't even work anymore. I still feel like a fraud. I'm just also hungover now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So if the drinking isn't actually solving the imposter syndrome — isn't canceling the noise like it used to — what do you think you'd actually need to address that part?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I think I need to talk to someone. Like regularly. Because I have all of this stuff running in my head — the comparison to other students, the feeling that my advisor is going to realize she made a mistake taking me on — and I've never actually... said it out loud to anyone who could help me work through it. I've just been drinking it quiet.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That makes a lot of sense. And just so you know — what you're describing, the imposter syndrome spiral, the using something external to cope with internal noise — that's something people work through in therapy all the time, and it responds really well to treatment. You're not a unique case of broken. You're a very common case of a smart person under enormous pressure without adequate support.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... actually really good to hear. I think I've been treating myself like I'm the only one who's ever felt this way and that there's something fundamentally wrong with me specifically. Which probably isn't helping.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If you imagine yourself a few months from now — getting some real support, having better tools for the anxiety, sleeping without the drinking — what does your relationship with the research look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to actually be in it again. Like — I used to get excited about my data. I'd be in the lab at weird hours because I wanted to be there, not because I was avoiding going home to a quiet apartment. I want that back. I miss it, actually. I didn't realize how much until right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You miss it. The version of yourself who was excited by the work — you haven't given up on him.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. No, I really haven't. I think that's why the ER thing scared me as much as it did. Like, in the back of my head I was thinking — if I let this keep going, I'm going to blow up the one thing I actually care about.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So given everything we've talked about today, what feels like a real first step — something you could actually do, not just something that sounds good to say?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Setting up regular sessions here, I think. And being honest with my advisor — like actually honest, not just 'I've been under some stress.' And maybe... not keeping alcohol in my apartment for a while. Just to see. Just to make it harder to reach for it automatically.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Those are concrete, thoughtful steps — not just vague intentions. And the fact that you can sit here, an hour after a genuinely hard few weeks, and think that clearly about what you need? That's real self-awareness. That's something to build on.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I wasn't expecting to feel like this coming in here. I thought you were going to lecture me or give me a pamphlet or something. But yeah. I think I can actually do this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So here's where we landed today. You came in after a scary night, a little reluctant, wanting me to know it wasn't as bad as it looked — and maybe part of you still isn't fully sure. But you also told me that the drinking stopped working, that your advisor's kindness hit you harder than any disappointment could, and that the guy who got into this program because he wanted to help people — he's still here and he wants his work back. You've got some clear steps in mind: regular sessions, honesty with your advisor, changing what's accessible at home. That's a solid start. How are you feeling heading out?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Lighter, actually. Which is weird because nothing's fixed yet. But yeah. Lighter.

client_context: A 42-year-old construction worker who drinks a six-pack every night. Referred by his doctor after abnormal liver tests. Thinks the doctor is overreacting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, thanks for joining today. I know telehealth can feel a little strange at first, so I appreciate you giving it a shot. There's no agenda here — you're in charge of where this goes. So... what brings you in today? What's on your mind?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? My doctor. She sent me here after some blood test came back weird. Said my liver numbers are high and I need to — quote — 'address my drinking.' Like, I don't even know why I'm on a video call right now. I drink a few beers after work. Every guy I know does.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it kind of feels like you got pushed into this. Like something got flagged, and now here you are — and you're not totally sure what you're even doing here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. I work construction. I'm on my feet all day, lifting stuff, dealing with the heat, dealing with the crew — a six-pack at night is not some big problem. That's just how you unwind. I've been doing it for twenty years. My dad did it. It's not like I'm falling down drunk or something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty years on the job — that's real, and it's hard. And it sounds like the six-pack at the end of the day isn't just about drinking. It's more like... the thing that finally lets you stop. Turn the switch off.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's it exactly. I don't even — like, I'm not craving it or whatever. It's just part of the routine. Come home, shower, crack one open, watch the game. My wife doesn't even say anything anymore. It's just... that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: On one hand, it's just the routine — the way things have always been, nothing out of the ordinary. And on the other hand... you're here. Your doctor's worried. Some part of you showed up today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — look, I only came because she said she'd flag it with my employer if I didn't do something. So it's not like I — I don't know. Those test results could mean anything, right? Like, maybe it's not even from the drinking. I take ibuprofen constantly for my back. That can mess up your liver too.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was it like when you first saw those numbers? When she actually sat you down and said your liver wasn't looking right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I don't know. I kind of brushed it off at first, like okay, whatever, let me get out of here. But then that night I was sitting there and I Googled it and... yeah. It was a little scarier than I wanted it to be. Cirrhosis, all that stuff. I didn't — I didn't say anything to my wife.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You sat with that alone. Looked it up, read what could happen... and it scared you. Even if you didn't let anyone else see that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm 42, you know? I got a kid in high school. I don't want to be sick. I don't want to be one of those guys who keels over at 55 and everyone's like, 'well, he should've seen it coming.' I just... I don't know how to — like, this is just my life, you know? I don't know what I'm supposed to do with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just take a moment to pull together what I'm hearing. You came in today because your doctor pushed you, and part of you wasn't sure any of this was necessary. You've worked hard for twenty years, and those beers at the end of the day have been the thing that's kept you going. At the same time, those test results hit you harder than you let on — and you've got a kid, a future you're thinking about. It sounds like there's a part of you that really doesn't want this to get worse.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I mean, when you put it like that. I'm not saying I'm gonna quit — I don't know if I even could, like, cold turkey or whatever. But maybe... maybe cutting back a little wouldn't be the end of the world. I don't know. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took something — saying that out loud. You walked in here not wanting to be here, and now you're sitting with the idea that something might be worth looking at. That matters. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want to end up sick. That's — that's the honest answer. I've seen guys go down that road and it's not pretty. I always figured it wouldn't be me, you know? But maybe it's at least worth... thinking about. Actually thinking about it.

client_context: A 45-year-old CEO who drinks a bottle of scotch nightly but maintains stellar work performance. Believes they have everything under control. Partner disagrees.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, good to see you. So last time we talked things were — cautiously optimistic, I think was the phrase. You had some momentum going. How's the week treated you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Fine. I mean — look, I'm going to get ahead of this before you do. It was a rough week. Couple of late nights, the drinking was... more than it had been. But I want to be clear, this was not some dramatic backslide. I had two deals closing simultaneously and a board presentation on Thursday. That's just the reality of the job. Anyone in my position would've done the same.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So before I even asked, you were already building the case. The week was brutal — real pressure, not imaginary — and the drinking matched it. And you want to make sure I don't turn that into something it isn't.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Because that's what happens here, right? One bad week becomes a pattern becomes a diagnosis. My CFO probably drank more than I did and nobody's sending him to... whatever this is. I run a company. I close deals. My numbers are better than they've ever been. If I had a problem — a real problem — you'd see it somewhere other than a glass of scotch at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The work is solid, the performance is solid — and yet you're here on a Tuesday morning instead of, I don't know, running a company. What's pulling you back in?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sarah. Mostly Sarah. She... she'd actually noticed. The past few weeks, before this week, she said something felt different. Said I seemed more present. That was — that actually meant something to me, hearing that. And then this week happened and I could see her face just... close back down. And I just — I don't know. I'm tired. I'm tired of being the guy who almost got there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The guy who almost got there. That's a hard thing to say out loud. And the fact that Sarah noticed real change — that landed. It mattered enough that losing that ground this week actually hurt.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it did. And I keep doing this thing where I tell myself it's situational — once Q2 closes, once the acquisition wraps, once things settle down. But there's always another Q2. There's always another acquisition. I've been saying 'once things settle' for about twelve years, so... I don't know what I'm waiting for, exactly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does it feel like to actually say that — that there's always going to be another 'once'?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? It feels like... Sarah keeps saying the scotch isn't a coping mechanism anymore, it's become the plan. I used to think that was her being dramatic — you know how she gets. But this week I thought about it and I couldn't really... I couldn't find the argument against it. Which is new. I always have an argument.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something shifted. The argument wasn't there. Was there a specific moment this week where you caught yourself and thought — huh.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Tuesday. The board call got pushed to Thursday and I poured a drink at like six PM just — just automatically. Didn't even think about it. The trigger wasn't even there yet. And I stood in the kitchen with the glass in my hand and I thought... this is interesting. Like, I was watching myself from the outside for a second. I've never really done that before. Or maybe I have and I just... looked away.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull this together, because I think there's more here than a rough week. You came in ready to defend yourself — which, honestly, fair, that's been the pattern — but underneath that, something real is happening. Sarah saw change and it mattered to you. You hit a wall this week and instead of just moving on, you noticed it. You stood in your kitchen and watched yourself. You couldn't find the argument. That's not a guy who's checked out. That's a guy who's starting to look.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I mean — yeah. I didn't build what I built by being someone who doesn't look at hard data. And maybe I've just been... very selectively ignoring this particular dataset for a long time. I don't want to be sixty and realize I traded everything that actually matters for a quarterly report and a bottle of Macallan. I don't want that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The guy who doesn't ignore hard data is sitting right here. So — what's one move this week? Not a plan, not a program. One thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Talking to Sarah. And not — not the version where I explain myself for forty-five minutes and she ends up comforting me. She keeps saying she wants her husband back, and I keep responding with a PowerPoint. Maybe I just... listen. Actually listen. That's probably where I should start.

client_context: An 18-year-old referred by school counselor after being caught drinking at a school event. Feels singled out since 'literally everyone drinks'.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this probably wasn't exactly how you wanted to spend your afternoon... I'm just wondering, what's it like being here right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? It's whatever. I'm only here because my mom basically forced me after the school called her, so. It's not like I actually need to be here. I didn't even do anything that bad. Literally everyone at that party was drinking, like everyone, and I'm the one who gets sent to a counselor. It's such a joke.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It really feels unfair. Like you got singled out when this is just... something everyone does.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. Thank you. Because no one gets that. My mom's acting like I showed up to school with a bottle of vodka or something, and it was like, a few sips at a football game. And people do way worse stuff than that all the time. I don't even drink that much, honestly. I just... I don't know, I don't want to be the weird one who doesn't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm. So part of it is about fitting in, not being on the outside... and you're sitting here feeling like the one person who got punished for something that's pretty normal in your world. I also want to say — it takes something to actually show up, even when you don't want to. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I guess. But I've done this before, okay? I saw a counselor in like, ninth grade, and it was pointless. She just kept asking how things made me feel and writing stuff down and nothing ever changed. So I don't really see why this is gonna be any different.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been through this before and it left you feeling like nothing actually got better. I'm curious — what would have needed to be different back then for it to have felt worth your time?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know... like, maybe if someone actually listened instead of just waiting for me to say something they could write in their little notepad. It felt like she already had the answer before I even walked in. Like she'd decided I was a problem and she just wanted me to admit it. And I'm not — I'm not a problem. I'm just... I'm trying to figure stuff out, same as everyone else.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You want someone to actually hear you. Not fix you, not hand you a label — just... hear what's actually going on for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, kind of... I mean, it's not like I never think about it. The drinking thing. Sometimes after, like, the next morning, I feel kind of... I don't know. Gross? Like it wasn't even that fun and I still did it. But it's hard to say no when you're there and everyone's doing it and you don't want to be the one standing in the corner by yourself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That morning-after feeling — that sounds like it's been sitting with you a little. What goes through your head in those moments?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... okay, this is gonna sound dumb, but I think about college a lot. Like, I worked really hard to get into a good school and my grades are actually good, and sometimes I'm like — what am I doing? My dad's whole thing growing up was 'don't be like me,' and he had a drinking problem when I was little so... I don't know. I don't think I have that, but sometimes I wonder if like... I don't know. Whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not dumb at all. That's actually really honest, and I imagine it's not easy to say that out loud. You've got these big things you're working toward, and somewhere underneath all of this, you're asking yourself a really important question.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess... yeah. I don't want to end up — I love my dad now, he's been sober for like six years, but I remember when I was little and it was really scary. And I keep telling myself I'm nothing like that. But like... I don't know why I can't just say no sometimes. That's the part I don't get about myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me make sure I'm understanding you. You came in here feeling like none of this was your problem — that you'd been unfairly called out when everyone else does the same thing. And that's still real. But as we've been talking, something else has come up too: those mornings after where something feels off, the worry about your future, what you saw growing up with your dad... and this question of why it feels so hard to choose differently in the moment. You're not here because someone else decided you're broken. You're here because part of you is actually asking something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I mean, when you say it like that. I didn't think I'd actually talk about any of this today. I figured I'd just sit here and wait for it to be over. But... maybe it's okay that I'm here. I don't know. Maybe.

client_context: A 24-year-old PhD student who has been drinking to manage thesis stress and imposter syndrome. Advisor noticed declining work quality.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So, last time we left off you were heading into a pretty high-stakes week. How did it go?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... yeah. Not great. My advisor basically tore apart my entire second chapter draft in lab meeting. Like, in front of everyone. The whole group just sitting there watching. I went home and I just — I don't know, I couldn't even look at my laptop. Just sat there. And yeah, I drank. More than I probably should have.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds genuinely humiliating. Being called out in front of your peers, the people you work alongside every day — and then coming home to that silence with nowhere to put it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. And the thing is, I'd worked on that chapter for like three weeks straight. Three weeks. I was sleeping four hours a night. And he just... I mean, he didn't even acknowledge any of the stuff that was good, you know? Just straight to the red pen. So I had a few drinks. And then a few more. And I basically lost two days. Missed a department seminar I was supposed to present at.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Missing that seminar — what did that stir up for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — honestly? I'm pissed. I'm really pissed. Because I'm not some undergrad who blew off a class. I had a whole presentation ready. And instead I'm emailing the coordinator at noon saying I'm 'unwell.' Which is technically true, I guess, but — god, this is so embarrassing to even say out loud. I worked so hard to get into this program and now I'm — what, hiding in my apartment because I can't handle a little criticism? It's pathetic.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to slow down on something you just said, because I think it matters. You called yourself pathetic. But what I'm actually hearing is someone who worked themselves to exhaustion trying to do good work, got blindsided publicly, and had no real outlet. That's not weakness. That's what happens when pressure has nowhere to go.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

I don't know. Maybe. But it's starting to — like, it's not staying contained anymore, that's what scares me. It used to just be Friday nights or whatever. Now it's... Sunday, Monday. I skipped a meeting with my advisor yesterday because I was still kind of hungover and I didn't want him to notice. And if he notices — if the department finds out — I could lose my funding. That would be it. Five years of this, gone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So underneath the anger at your advisor, at the situation — there's this fear that the thing you're using to cope is quietly becoming the threat itself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's a good way to put it. Because I'm not stupid, I know what I'm doing when I open the bottle. In the moment it just — it quiets everything down. The imposter syndrome, the 'you don't belong here' voice, all of it just... shuts off. But then I wake up and I've lost a day and the work is still there and now I'm also behind and also feel like garbage. So it's like I'm borrowing against myself, and the interest rate is getting higher.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really sharp observation about yourself. You understand the mechanics of it. So let me ask you this — when you picture yourself two years from now, finishing this dissertation, defending it, whatever that looks like — what's actually driving that picture for you? What made you want this in the first place?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
I mean... I grew up watching my dad work a job he hated for thirty years. He's brilliant, like actually brilliant, but he never got the chance. And I always thought — I'm going to do the thing that matters. Research that actually changes how people think about something. I picked this field because I genuinely find it fascinating. Not for the money, obviously. 

I don't... I haven't thought about that version of myself in a while. It feels far away right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I've heard today, and you tell me if I'm getting it right. You had a brutal week — a public hit to your work, your confidence, and then two lost days that cost you professionally in a way that really scared you. And you're scared not because you don't care, but because you care deeply. About the research, about what it means to you, about honoring something your father didn't get. And you're starting to see that what's been helping you survive the stress is starting to work against the very thing that gives you a reason to push through.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's — I mean, when you say it back like that it seems pretty clear, doesn't it. Like I've been running from the fire by running into the building or something. I don't want to keep losing days. I really don't. I think... I think I actually need to figure out a different way to handle this. The drinking isn't working anymore, it's just — it's delaying things and making them worse.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Given everything you just said — what feels like the most important first step for you? Not what you think you should say, just what actually feels real.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly... I think I need to tell someone I trust what's actually going on. Not the 'I've been stressed' version. The real version. Maybe my friend Priya, she's in the program too. And I want to actually try that thing we talked about last time — the structured writing blocks where I stop at a set time no matter what, instead of just grinding until I hate myself. I can't keep using the stress as a reason to drink and then drinking as a reason to be more stressed. That's not — that's not the person I want to be.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again, Marcus. Come on in, sit wherever you want. How've things been since we last met?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... alright. Better than before, I guess. Not that it matters what I say in here — you're writing stuff down either way, right?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said 'better than before.' I'm curious what better looks like for you these days.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I actually — okay, I didn't drink for three weeks. Three whole weeks. First time in... I don't even know how long. And I'm not saying it's because of any of this. I'm just saying it happened.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three weeks. That's real. Something shifted for you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well... then the thing with my brother happened and I — look, I don't want to get into the whole thing. It's complicated. It's always complicated with him.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't have to go into all of it if you're not ready. But when the thing with your brother hit — what was going on for you inside, in that moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He calls out of nowhere saying he needs money, and I know what that means. He's using again. And I just... I felt like, what's the point, you know? Like I'm trying to hold my stuff together and everything around me is still just... falling apart.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Like you'd been holding things together on your end, and then this just pulled the rug out.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And then I drank. Okay? I'm just gonna say it — I drank. Two nights. And now you're gonna put that in your report and send it to the court and that's it, I'm done.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I hear that you're scared about what this means. And I want you to notice something — you just told me straight, no dancing around it. That takes something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What does it take? It takes being stuck in a situation where I've got no other option. This whole thing is a joke. Two DUIs and suddenly I'm — I'm some kind of dangerous criminal that needs to be fixed.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The system feels like it's treating you as a problem to be managed, not a person. What is it you think they're getting wrong about who you are?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never hurt anybody. Both times I was — I wasn't even driving crazy. I just... I never hurt a single person. But they look at me like I'm some kind of monster.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't see yourself as someone who hurts people. And it sounds like, underneath all this anger at the court... there's a part of you that knows the drinking hasn't been working for you. For a while now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... My daughter doesn't call me. She's sixteen and she doesn't — she won't pick up. I text her and she just... leaves it. That's not what I wanted. That's not what I wanted for her.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a painful thing to sit with. What does it mean to you that she's pulled away?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It means I screwed up. I know that. I'm not an idiot. I just... I come here, I do the sessions, I white-knuckle three weeks and I still don't — I don't know how to fix any of it. I don't know what I'm even doing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're putting in real effort and it still feels like the pieces aren't coming back together. Like the work you're doing isn't reaching the thing that actually hurts.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, exactly. And then I slip and I think... why am I even bothering. Why bother at all.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just try to pull together what I'm hearing, make sure I've got it right. You had three weeks — real weeks — where you didn't drink. Then your brother called, it hit that old feeling of 'what's the point,' and you drank for two nights. Now you're carrying fear about the court, grief about your daughter, and this question of whether trying is even worth it. And in the middle of all that... you still showed up today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I showed up because I have to. ... But I mean. Yeah. I don't know. Maybe a little because I — I want to know if it's actually possible. To be different. I've never really... I've never actually thought about it that way before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would 'different' look like for you — not for the court, not for your daughter — just for Marcus?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Just... waking up and not feeling like garbage. Not feeling like one phone call away from everything blowing up. Being someone who — who's got his head on straight. I don't know if that's even possible for me at this point but... maybe. Maybe it is.
